title: Thiebou Dieune Bou Wekh
author: MAGGI Sénégal
desc: The white version with the soul buried in the rice fifteen minutes in — and a published ingredient list carrying several misprints this entry reproduces rather than fixes.
longDesc: A Senegalese-market institutional recipe for the white ceebu jen, included because sources for the white version are scarce. A kilo of long-grain white rice and a kilo and a half of smoked fish, with carrots, turnip leaves, eggplant, cassava at fifty grams each and two hundred grams of fresh okra. The roof stuffing is pounded parsley, onion, chilli and half a bouillon tablet. The soul — the nététou ball — is buried in the rice after fifteen minutes of its forty-minute cook and covered back over. The béguète is bissap leaves boiled and crushed with okra. Its printed ingredient list contains several evident machine-translation artifacts, flagged below and left as printed.
ingredients: 1 kg long-grain white rice, regular, raw, enriched
2 cloves garlic — the page prints 'Ail : 2 Les chefs', a misprint, see the note
1 tbsp of a meatless bacon-bits line that appears to be a database artifact — see the note
1 portion dried fish standing in for guedj — see the note (SEN088)
// Plus, from the method: nététou seeds for the soul, and bissap leaves for the béguète
equipment: Couscoussier — the page calls it an indé
steps: Make the roof: pound parsley, onion, chilli and half the bouillon tablet. Stuff the fish with it.
Make a second farce with parsley, chilli, onion, bell pepper and the rest of the tablet.
Fry the onions, the nokoss and the tomato pulp 5 minutes.
Add 1 to 1.5 litres of water, the vegetables, the fish and the okra, and leave it to simmer a good hour.
Soak the nététou seeds to remove the skins, pound them with onion and dried chillies, form one large ball and set it aside.
Wash and stem the bissap leaves, boil them, and crush them with okra. Add 2 or 3 tablespoons of broth and set aside. Done when the leaves are well cooked.
Steam the rice in the couscoussier about 10 minutes.
Remove the fish and vegetables with a little broth and keep them warm.
Pour the broth over the rice so it just covers, cover, lower the heat and cook 40 minutes.
After 15 minutes, dig a hole in the rice, bury the ball of soul, cover it over and finish the cooking.
Serve with the soumbara and the sorrel-and-okra mix.
chefTips: Burying the soul in the rice partway through the cook is the technique worth taking from this recipe — fifteen minutes into forty, so it steams inside the grain rather than sitting on top.
Broth poured so it JUST covers the rice. The same instruction appears in every well-made Senegalese rice dish and it is the difference between grains and porridge.
When the leaves are well cooked is the only true sensory cue on the page. Everything else is a clock.
Steam the rice ten minutes before it meets the broth, in a couscoussier if you have one.

Treat the printed ingredient list with care — several lines are evident machine-translation or food-database artifacts, including a meatless-bacon line and an Alaskan whitefish line standing in for guedj. They are reproduced above because this collection does not silently correct sources, but they are not what a Senegalese cook would use.
The site's own displayed timers of 170, 45, 20, 15 and 90 minutes do not map onto any step in its text. Follow the in-text times.
For a version of the white ceebu jen from a named Senegalese cook rather than an institutional source, SEN004 is the one to read.
commonMistakes: Adding the soul at the start or at the end rather than at the fifteen-minute mark.
Following the site's displayed timers rather than its text.
Taking the misprinted ingredient lines literally.
Under-cooking the bissap leaves for the béguète.
sources: Adapted from 'Thiebou Dieune Bou Wekh', MAGGI Sénégal — page title 'Préparez un Délicieux Thiebou Dieune Bou Wekh | MAGGI'. BYLINE: NONE. DATE: NONE; the most recent comments on the page are dated 17-12-2025. SO THIS IS AN ORGANISATION-ONLY SOURCE (MAGGI Sénégal / Nestlé) AND IS FLAGGED PROMINENTLY AS SUCH. It is published because it is a Senegalese-market, French-language institutional source for the WHITE variant, which is genuinely scarce — not because a brand page is a good recipe source. Portions as printed: 'Ce plat a été optimisé pour 6 portions.' Difficulty as printed: Difficile. Total duration displayed: 170 Min. TWO-PASS.

Ingredient list as printed in French, INCLUDING the garbled lines, which are NOT corrected: 'Riz blanc à grain long, régulier, cru, enrichi : 1 kilogramme'; 'Poisson fumé :' — pass one read '1,5 kilogramme' and pass two '1.5 kilogrammes', a decimal-separator rendering difference, BOTH READINGS REPORTED AND NEITHER RECONCILED; 'Carottes : 50 g'; 'Feuilles de navet, crues : 50 g'; 'Aubergine : 50 g'; 'Manioc, cru : 50 g'; 'Gombo frais : 200 g'; 'Oignons : 2 Médiums'; 'Ail : 2 Les chefs'; 'Poivron rouge : 1 Petit'; 'Tomates fraîches : 1 Moyen'; 'Morceaux de bacon, sans viande : 1 à soupe'; 'Poisson, corégone, séché (natif de l'Alaska) : 1'; 'Persil : 1 bouquet'; 'Pâte de tomate : 100 g'; 'huile d'olive : 4 à soupe'; 'Piments, piments rouges, rouges, crus : 2 pièces'; 'Tamarin, cru : 250 g'; 'MAGGI Tablette : 10 g'; 'MAGGI Mameum Epices : 10 g'.

FOUR SUSPECTED MISPRINTS, each reproduced as printed and flagged rather than fixed. (1) 'Ail : 2 Les chefs' — evidently for '2 gousses', two cloves; 'Les chefs' appears to be a machine-translation artifact. (2) 'Morceaux de bacon, sans viande : 1 à soupe' — meatless bacon bits in a Senegalese fish dish, with a malformed unit apparently for '1 c. à soupe'. (3) 'Poisson, corégone, séché (natif de l'Alaska) : 1' — dried Alaskan whitefish, evidently a food-database row standing in for GUEDJ, with a quantity of '1' carrying no unit at all. (4) 'huile d'olive : 4 à soupe' — malformed unit. Also recorded: 'Piments, piments rouges, rouges, crus' triplicates a word, and the page writes 'Mameum' in the ingredient list and 'Mameun' in the step-4 card, BOTH SPELLINGS REPORTED.

A TIMER INCONSISTENCY, flagged: the site displays timers of 170, 45, 20, 15 and 90 minutes that do NOT map onto any step. The in-text times are 5 minutes, about an hour, about 10 minutes, 40 minutes, and the 15-minute point at which the soul is buried. The in-text times are the ones followed above.

DONENESS CUES as printed in French: 'laisser mijoter une bonne heure'; 'faire cuire à la vapeur environ 10 min'; 'laisser cuire 40 minutes'; and 'Quand les feuilles sont bien cuites' for the bissap leaves — THE ONLY TRUE SENSORY CUE ON THE PAGE. The soul and the béguète both carry NO time at all, absent.

NUTRITION AS PRINTED PER PORTION, which is why the calorie figure on this entry is so much higher than its neighbours and is the source's own rather than this collection's estimate: 'Glucides 176,48 g; Énergie 1 314,82 kcal; Lipides 41,25 g; Protéines 57,21 g.'

CULTURAL FRAMING as printed: 'plat sénégalais traditionnel'; nététou described as fermented néré seeds, a traditional Senegalese condiment. The local terms nokoss, guedj, yett and soumbara all appear on the page unexplained.

A READER SHOULD TREAT THIS as the weakest-sourced entry in the Senegalese rice dishes: no byline, no date, a brand publisher, and four misprints in twenty ingredient lines. It earns its place only because the white ceebu jen is otherwise documented just once, at SEN004.
reheating: Steam the rice; warm the fish and vegetables in broth.
healthBenefits: Very high in protein, at the source's own figure of 57 g per portion.
Nététou contributes fermented plant protein and B vitamins.
Okra and turnip leaves add soluble fibre and folate.
culturalNote: Bouillon-cube brands publish recipes in West Africa because their product is genuinely in almost every pot, and a Senegalese-market page for the white ceebu jen is a real document of how the dish is cooked now. It is also a reminder to read any brand recipe with one eye on the ingredient list, which here has wandered through a translation engine.
